label: Braids
notes: Open the lecture. Braids give an algebraic handle on knots and links. The lecture introduces the braid group, its generators and relations, the closure operation that turns braids into links, and the theorems of Alexander and Markov that connect braid algebra to knot theory in a precise dictionary.

label: The Braid Group
notes: Define a braid on n strands as a collection of descending strings joining n top points to n bottom points, considered up to isotopy. Stacking braids defines a group operation, with the identity the trivial braid and inverses obtained by flipping upside down. This is Artin's braid group on n strands.

label: Generators and Relations
notes: Present the standard generators, each swapping two adjacent strands with a fixed crossing sign. They satisfy two relations: distant swaps commute, and adjacent generators obey the braid relation. These finitely many relations present the entire braid group and encode all isotopies between braids in a purely algebraic form.

label: Closing a Braid
notes: Describe the closure: join each top endpoint to the corresponding bottom endpoint by arcs around the side, turning a braid into an oriented link diagram. Alexander's theorem asserts that every link arises as the closure of some braid, so braids capture all of knot and link theory.

label: Markov's Theorem
notes: State Markov's theorem: two braids, possibly on different numbers of strands, have isotopic closures exactly when they are related by a finite sequence of conjugations and stabilizations. This converts the topological problem of equivalence of links into the algebraic problem of these two Markov moves on braid words.

label: Recap
notes: Close the lecture. The braid group is generated by adjacent transpositions subject to the braid relation, every link is a braid closure by Alexander, and Markov's theorem characterizes when two closures agree. This algebraic dictionary underlies trace constructions of the Jones polynomial. The next lecture turns to discriminants and finite type invariants.
